clinicalPearls: Dientamoeba fragilis is a trichomonad-related flagellate that, despite its name, has no external flagella and historically no recognised cyst stage, existing chiefly as a fragile trophozoite
It is a common colonic protozoan whose pathogenic role is debated, but it is increasingly linked to chronic non-bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, bloating and anorexia, especially in children
Peripheral eosinophilia can accompany infection, an unusual feature among enteric protozoa
It is thought to be co-transmitted with the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis, whose eggs may serve as a protective vehicle for the delicate trophozoite
The trophozoite typically has two nuclei, and the organism degenerates rapidly in stool, so prompt fixation and permanent staining greatly improve detection
Routine wet-mount microscopy frequently misses it; permanent stained smears or molecular PCR are far more sensitive
Metronidazole is commonly used for symptomatic infection, and concurrent treatment of coexisting pinworm should be considered
reference.pathophysiology: Dientamoeba fragilis is a flagellate protozoan that colonises the lumen and mucosal surface of the large intestine without demonstrable tissue invasion. The trophozoite is osmotically fragile and does not survive well outside the host, and a robust cyst stage has not been reliably demonstrated, which has long puzzled parasitologists regarding its transmission. The leading hypothesis is that it is carried within the eggs of the pinworm Enterobius vermicularis, explaining frequent co-infection. Mucosal irritation and mild inflammation, rather than invasion, are thought to underlie the abdominal pain and diarrhoea attributed to symptomatic infection, and an eosinophilic response may occur.
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy using permanent stained smears rather than wet mount alone
Prompt fixation of stool given rapid trophozoite degeneration
Molecular PCR, which is highly sensitive
Perianal tape test for coexisting pinworm
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia
Testing to exclude other enteric pathogens in persistent symptoms
redFlags: Persistent symptoms despite treatment, prompting reassessment for another diagnosis
Weight loss or growth faltering in an affected child
Bloody diarrhoea or systemic features atypical for this organism
Failure to eradicate infection suggesting reinfection from untreated pinworm
reference.prognosis: Benign overall; symptomatic infection generally responds well to antiprotozoal treatment, though relapse or persistence can occur if coexisting pinworm infection is not also addressed.
pitfalls: Relying on wet-mount microscopy alone, which frequently fails to detect the fragile trophozoite
Delaying stool fixation so the organism degenerates before examination
Overlooking and failing to treat concurrent pinworm infection
Attributing all symptoms to Dientamoeba without considering functional bowel disorders
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat symptomatic infection with an antiprotozoal agent such as metronidazole, paromomycin or iodoquinol
Identify and treat coexisting Enterobius vermicularis pinworm infection to prevent relapse, as it is thought to co-transmit the organism
Confirm the diagnosis with prompt stool fixation and permanent stained smears or molecular PCR rather than wet mount alone
Provide supportive symptomatic care for diarrhoea and abdominal pain with attention to hydration
Exclude other enteric pathogens where symptoms persist despite treatment
Reassess and re-treat for persistence or relapse, ensuring coexisting pinworm is also addressed
